::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Why does the direction of the gradient vector depend only on the tangent vector to the contour and not the nature of the function itself?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5089348/why-does-the-direction-of-the-gradient-vector-depend-only-on-the-tangent-vector), asked by [HPB](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/797768/hpb) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2025-08-11; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Consider a function $z = f(x,y)$.
>
> The gradient vector (which gives the direction along which the function $f$ will change the fastest) is said to be perpendicular to the tangent vector at any point on the plane curve (which is a contour, ie, the value of $z$ stays the same on that curve, for all $x$ and $y$). And this direction of the gradient vector is true irrespective of the definition of $f$.
>
> I understand all the calculations and the proofs, but intuitively it doesn't make sense. If I am standing on a plane curve / contour of a mountain range, and I'm facing the tangent vector at that point, the rate of the greatest change should surely depend on the nature of the function $f$, ie, in this case, the terrain? For example, I might find that 30 degrees to my right there is a very steep slope up, and 90 degrees to the tangent vector the terrain only rises by a tiny bit. In which case that 30 degree would be the direction along which the maximum change to $f$ would take place - not perpendicular to the tangent vector.
>
> Where am I going wrong?
:::

You need to assume that the mountain is the graph of a differentiable function. One way to think about differentiability at a point is that all the partial derivatives exist, and the affine-linear function they determine is a “really good” approximation to the function near the point. If the partial derivatives are continuous, then the function is differentiable, and the level curves will also be differentiable.

The situation you're describing sounds continuous, but not differentiable.

For example, let $f(x,y) = \frac{3x^2y + y^3}{x^2 + y^2}$ if $(x,y) \neq (0,0)$, and $f(0,0) = 0$. This function is graphed below. It looks very similar to the graph that @Carmeister created. 

[![graph of f][1]][1]

The level curve $f=0$ is the $x$-axis. The partial derivatives of $f$ at $(0,0)$ are
$$\begin{align*}
    \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)
&= \lim_{x\to 0} \frac{f(x,0)}{x} = \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{0}{x} = 0 
\\\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)
&= \lim_{y\to 0} \frac{f(0,y)}{y} = \lim_{y\to 0}\frac{y}{y} = 1 
\end{align*}$$
So $\nabla f(0,0) = \left<0,1\right>$.

To find the direction of greatest increase, first let's compute the directional derivative in an arbitrary direction $\left<\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right>$. We have
$$\begin{align*}
   D_{\left<\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right>}f(0,0)
   &= \lim_{t\to 0} \frac{f(t\cos\theta,t\sin\theta)}{t}
 \\&= \lim_{t\to 0} \frac{1}{t}\left(\frac{t^3 (3\cos^2\theta \sin \theta + \sin^3 \theta)}{t^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2 \theta)}\right) 
  \\&= 3\cos^2\theta \sin \theta + \sin^3 \theta
  \\&= 3 \sin\theta - 2 \sin^3 \theta
\end{align*}$$
To find the extreme values of this directional derivative, we take *its* derivative with respect to $\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}
   \frac{d}{d\theta} D_{\left<\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right>}f(0,0)
   &= 3\cos\theta - 6 \sin^2 \theta \cos \theta
  \\&= 3\cos\theta\left(1 - 2 \sin^2 \theta\right)
\end{align*}$$
The critical points are where $\cos\theta = 0$ or $\sin^2\theta = \frac{1}{2}$.

 * If $\cos\theta = 0$, then $\sin\theta = \pm 1$, and $2 \sin\theta - \sin^3 \theta = \pm 1$.
 * If $\sin^2\theta = \frac{1}{2}$, then $3 \sin\theta - 2\sin^3 \theta = \pm \sqrt{2}$, depending on the sign of $\sin\theta$. 

So $D_{\left<\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right>}f(0,0)$ achieves its maximum of $\sqrt{2}$ at $\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{4}$, and its minimum of $-\sqrt{2}$ at $-\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $-\frac{3\pi}{4}$. The angles $\theta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}$ are critical, and they are perpendicular to the level curve, but they are not global extrema. In fact $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ is a local minimum and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ is a local maximum. You can see this on the graph, and verify it using the second derivative test. Here is a graph of $D_{\left<\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right>}f(0,0)$ versus $\theta$:

[![graph of directional derivative][2]][2]

Finally, we can see why this doesn't violate the “gradient points in direction of greatest increase” rule. $f$ is differentiable at $(0,0)$ if and only if 
$$\lim_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}
    \frac{f(x,y) - f(0,0) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0)x - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0)y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} = 0$$
We have $f(0,0) = 0$, $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) = 0$, and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(0,0) = 1$. So we want to find the limit of
$$\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\left[\frac{3x^2y+y^2}{x^2+y^2} - y \right]
&= \frac{3x^2y + y^3 - y^2(x^2+y^2)}{(x^2+y^2)^{3/2}}
\\&= \frac{2x^2y}{(x^2+y^2)^{3/2}}
\end{align*}$$
If we approach $(0,0)$ along the line $x = t$, $y= 0$, the limit will be $0$. But if we approach $(0,0)$ along the line $x=t$, $y=t$, the limit will be $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. So the two-variable limit cannot exist. This means $f$ is *not* differentiable at $(0,0)$.
